concept.rationale: Figure 2 more truthfully represents the requested supervised-learning loss landscape: Panel A uses Intercept φ0 over 0–2 and Slope φ1 over 0–4, computes a quadratic least-squares-style loss surface from data, and encodes the minimum as the lightest/near-white region with increasingly teal higher loss, matching the core concepts in the brief (L00007). Figure 1 is conceptually worse because its Panel A slope axis and controls run from about -1 to 1 rather than 0 to 4, and its loss coloring uses a dark/orange minimum with bright high-loss regions, contradicting the specified near-white low-loss-to-teal high-loss encoding and risking a wrong understanding of the parameter landscape (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall reconstruction: it more faithfully preserves the two-panel layout, loss-landscape appearance, contour/path structure, scatterplot with fitted-line evolution, and most labels/numbered annotations, whereas Figure 2 changes the panel-a styling and geometry substantially and has missing or clipped labels. Figure 2 is better on the authored interaction/concept ranges for the sliders and slope parameter, but relative to Figure 1 it is visually and geometrically less faithful to the target figure, with distorted parameter-space proportions, omitted trajectory arrowheads/curved evolution cues, and weaker labeling.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 and Figure 2 both use the correct six original vertices, eight original edges, and generate the line-graph connections between edge-nodes that share an original endpoint, but Figure 1 is structurally closer because it preserves the full construction sequence with a distinct intermediate state where the new edge-graph edges are added over a faded original graph. Figure 2 has the same underlying topology, but its teal nodes are relatively oversized and it jumps directly from added edge-nodes to the final edge graph, losing one structural stage and making the reconstruction less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 has more complete and coherent controls: its Prev/Next and radio phase handlers update the construction state, provide a separate edge-node connection phase, clear stale selections on phase changes, and generally prevent interaction with invisible nodes/edges. Figure 2’s basic step buttons work, but it collapses the connection step into the final edge-graph state, leaves invisible teal nodes and original-edge hit areas clickable in states where they are hidden, and does not provide as clean a way to click a visible original edge while seeing the generated line-graph connections.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 more closely matches the reference panel a at a glance: the orange node color, heavier black edges, larger labeled circles, and especially the geometry with node 1 above node 6 and a nearly vertical 1–6 edge resemble the original graph better. Figure 2 shows the same graph, but its thinner strokes, smaller nodes, and more skewed layout make it look less like the textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has better label quality because it explicitly includes the matching panel label text “a) Original graph” and its node labels are clear and uncluttered. Figure 1’s node labels are also readable, but the important original title/panel label is only indirectly represented in a sidebar radio list, while much of its visible text consists of invented UI annotations that do not match the textbook figure and add clutter.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly implement the central line-graph rule: original undirected edges become teal nodes and new edges are drawn exactly when the corresponding original edges share an endpoint (L00007). Figure 2 teaches this more accurately because its three displayed steps are explicitly labeled as a) Original graph, b) Add edge-nodes, and c) Edge graph, matching the brief’s three-panel conceptual structure and titles; Figure 1’s underlying graph transformation is also correct, but it reframes the construction as four phases and does not explicitly present the requested a/b/c panel labeling, making the textbook concept slightly less directly represented (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it better preserves the graph geometry and visual appearance of the reference and provides a more complete construction sequence, including a distinct phase where line-graph connections are added over the faded original graph. Compared with Figure 1, Figure 2 has clearer textbook-style panel labels and a concise three-step framing, but it loses an intermediate structural step, has weaker interaction behavior with hidden/clickable elements, and its layout/styling is less faithful to the original rendering.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the original DCGAN architecture geometry: it uses a full sequence of proportionally changing 3D cuboids with increasing spatial face size and decreasing channel depth, includes the thin image plane with a textured front face, preserves the generator/discriminator grouping with curly braces, and places the operation annotations and diagonal arrows in a layout closer to the source. Figure 2 has the same basic block count, but its oblique/front-on projection makes the diagram flatter, its bridge arrow and operation arrows are spatially less faithful, the output image is only a grey grid plane, and the bracket/arrow structure is more schematic than the original.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 handles the requested generator and discriminator traces more robustly: each button cleanly resets a single animation state, highlights the correct successive tensor blocks, and updates a caption with the current stage and tensor size. Figure 1 also traces both passes with a moving marker and highlight, but repeated clicks can start multiple overlapping requestAnimationFrame loops because old animation callbacks are not cancelled, and it provides less explicit feedback about which architectural operation or tensor stage is currently being shown.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more faithful at a glance because it preserves the original's left-to-right generator/discriminator layout, horizontal grouping braces, brown block color scheme, central image, and main dimensional labels. Figure 1 contains the same ingredients but the strong oblique perspective makes the whole diagram collapse into a diagonal, with braces and labels badly skewed/overlapping, so it reads less like the clean textbook architecture.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has labels that are generally better placed and closer to the reference layout, with clearer Generator/Discriminator headings and most layer-size and operation labels readable despite some crowding. Figure 1 includes the main labels but many are distorted by perspective, collide with blocks or each other, and the rightmost sigmoid/Pr(real)/1×1 labels are especially cluttered and hard to read.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the generator as a 100×1 latent vector projected to 4×4×1024 and then upsampled by fractional convolutions through 8×8×512, 16×16×256, 32×32×128, and 64×64×3, whereas Figure 2 misleadingly labels the final 32×32×128→64×64×3 generator transition as only “arctan” and brackets fractional convolution over only the earlier upsampling stages, which misstates the operation sequence described in the brief (L00007). Both figures capture the discriminator’s downsampling sequence and final 4×4 convolution plus sigmoid to Pr(real), but Figure 1’s operation labels are less misleading overall, even though it omits explicit arctan activation labels that Figure 2 at least attempts to include (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because its rendered diagram is much clearer and closer to the textbook-style left-to-right layout, with more readable headings, dimensional labels, grouping braces, and a central image, while Figure 1’s oblique perspective causes skewed braces, overlapping labels, and clutter around the discriminator output. Figure 2 also provides more robust interaction traces with clean resets and stage captions, whereas Figure 1 can start overlapping animations and gives less explicit feedback. Figure 1 is better in source-level architectural geometry and avoids Figure 2’s misleading generator operation labeling, but those advantages do not outweigh Figure 2’s clearer presentation and more reliable interaction behavior.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the full four-panel structure: the 6-node/7-edge graph, 6×6 adjacency matrix, 5×6 node-feature matrix, and 4×7 edge-feature matrix are all visible at once with proportions and label placement closer to the likely textbook layout. Figure 2 has the same basic topology and matrix counts, but it compresses the figure vertically, adds extra panel background boxes, places some titles differently, and initially dims the matrix panels so the reconstructed full structure is less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements all three intended interaction types: graph node clicks update the adjacency and node-data representations via dimming, graph edge clicks emphasize the edge data column and endpoints, and the panel-focus selector/step controls correctly switch attention among panels a–d. Figure 1 handles node and edge highlighting more explicitly with outlines and synchronized dropdowns, but it does not provide any real panel toggle/comparison control, so it misses a major requested interaction; its step buttons only cycle selections, not panels.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the overall multi-panel composition of the reference: the graph on the left, adjacency and node-data matrices above/right, and edge-data matrix below, with similar colors and labeling. Figure 2 renders the graph panel larger but fades the other panels heavily and even clips the leftmost node area, so the overall figure is less immediately recognizable as the original textbook layout.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 preserves the full set of panel labels and matrix annotations from the reference, including the adjacency, node data, and edge data labels, whereas Figure 2 fades most non-focused labels so strongly that b), c), d) and their matrix annotations are barely readable or effectively missing. Although Figure 1's labels are small at inline size, Figure 2 also clips/crowds the visual graph area and makes many required labels too faint, so Figure 1 is better overall for label completeness and readability.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 teaches the core encodings more accurately because it explicitly states that the adjacency matrix is N × N, filled cells indicate edges, and the undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix, and it correctly describes X and E as column-wise feature matrices ordered by nodes and edges (L00007). Figure 1 has the same correct topology and matrix shapes, but it leaves more of these relationships implicit and its edge-to-E ordering is less clearly explained; both figures share the minor notation mismatch of labeling edge features as D_E × E rather than the brief’s Dᴷ × E (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall reconstruction because it preserves the full four-panel textbook layout, visible matrices, graph placement, and label completeness more faithfully than Figure 2. Figure 2 has better implemented panel-focus interactions and more explicit conceptual explanations, but relative to Figure 1 it fades or obscures key matrix panels and labels and even crowds/clips part of the graph, making the complete figure less recognizable and less readable.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately reconstructs the textbook geometry because it shows the two required panels side by side: a 3D loss surface with wall grids and a separate heatmap/contour plot, with axis ranges and loss ticks matching the apparent 0–2, -1–1, and 0/35/70 structure. Figure 2 instead collapses the concept into a single toggleable plot, uses a different quadratic loss landscape and minimum, different tick spacing on the loss axis, and a perspective/top-down transition rather than the printed simultaneous surface-plus-heatmap layout, so its spatial relationships and element count are substantially less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the requested core interactions more directly: dragging the current marker updates both the 3D surface and heatmap marker, recomputes the displayed loss, resets the path, and automatically animates gradient descent, while the learning-rate slider restarts the descent using the new step size. Figure 2 has useful extra controls, but its drag only changes the start point and leaves descent idle unless the separate Run button is pressed, the learning-rate slider merely changes a value without recomputing or restarting the path when idle, and its large-rate behavior is distorted by silently clamping parameters to the allowed box rather than showing the actual overshooting dynamics. Figure 1 is not perfect because extreme learning rates can terminate abruptly when the iterate leaves the plotted region, but Figure 2’s controls less reliably produce the advertised effects.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is much more visually recognizable as the original loss landscape: it shows a large brown convex 3D surface with grid/axis structure and colored parameter markers, whereas Figure 1 renders both panels so tiny and cluttered that the actual geometry and heatmap are barely legible. Figure 1 does include both the surface and contour view, but its severe scaling and overlapping labels make it much less faithful at a glance than Figure 2’s clearer single-panel recreation.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has more readable and less cluttered axis labels on the 3D surface, with labels like Intercept, φ0 and Loss, L[φ] placed more cleanly, whereas Figure 1’s labels are extremely small, heavily overlapping, and clustered so that both panel labels and axis text are difficult to read. Figure 1 does attempt both a) and b), but its label placement is poor and it also includes distracting UI text; Figure 2 is missing the full two-panel labeling of the reference and has some extra UI/annotation text, but its actual plot labels are substantially clearer.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the brief because it shows both the 3D quadratic loss surface and the corresponding top-down heatmap over the same parameter plane, with matching colored markers in both views and consistent axes for phi_0, phi_1, and loss 0–70 (L00007-L00010). Its quadratic is convex with a visible single global minimum and no local minima or saddle points, matching the least-squares loss-landscape concept (L00011-L00014). Figure 2 also uses a convex quadratic with sensible parameter ranges, but it replaces the two-panel comparison with a single morphing/toggled view rather than asserting the same markers simultaneously in both panels, so it teaches the correspondence between surface and heatmap less directly and less faithfully to the stated concept (L00007-L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall match because it preserves the intended two-panel structure—a 3D loss surface alongside a corresponding heatmap/contour view—with consistent markers, axes, and loss-scale behavior, whereas Figure 2 collapses this into a single toggleable/morphing plot with a different landscape and less faithful spatial layout. Figure 1 also implements the core interactive behavior more directly, updating linked markers and restarting descent when parameters or learning rate change, while Figure 2 often requires a separate run action and clamps overshooting behavior. Figure 2 is visually clearer and has more readable labels, but those rendering advantages do not outweigh Figure 1’s stronger geometric, conceptual, and interaction fidelity.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 reconstructs the pinhole-camera geometry much more accurately: the camera body/projection plane is centered about the optical axis, the pinhole lies at the center of the near face, the focal-length dimension runs correctly from projection plane to camera center, and the X/Y/Z axes have the intended spatial relationship under an oblique view. Figure 2 shifts the box entirely to one side in depth, putting the pinhole on an edge/corner of the camera box rather than centered on the face and making the optical/principal axis miss the center of the projection plane; it also uses a narrower, off-center projection plane and less complete/less accurate cuboid edge geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the requested handedness toggle with a coherent axis flip and updated explanatory sign convention, and its registered hitboxes correctly highlight the projection plane, pinhole, optical axis, and focal length with popups. Figure 1’s available slider and transparency checkbox mostly work, but they are not the requested interactions, it lacks the right/left-handed convention toggle and all click-to-highlight component interactions, and its focal-length slider can change the geometry without refitting the view at extremes.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the reference’s recognizable translucent 3D camera volume with distinct blue/green/dark faces, the pinhole on the side, the world-coordinate axes, dashed construction lines, labels, and the red focal-length arrow in a similar composition. Figure 2 captures the basic pinhole-camera idea and labels, but its geometry is flatter and more simplified, the color scheme is much less like the original, and it loses much of the layered cuboid/projection-plane appearance that makes the textbook figure recognizable.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the required diagram labels more legibly placed, with less collision between text and geometry: 'Projection plane,' 'Pinhole camera,' 'World coordinates,' axis letters, 'Optical / principal axis,' 'Pinhole / camera center,' and 'f' are all readable and reasonably close to their targets. Figure 1 includes the same main labels, but several are smaller and more cluttered, especially the optical-axis and pinhole-center labels which crowd the cube and axes, making them harder to read at inline size.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more conceptually accurate because its pinhole is placed at the center of the camera rear face and its X, Y, Z arrows form a right-handed frame with Y upward and f spanning between the labeled projection-plane side and the pinhole, matching the core naming geometry better (L00010). Figure 2 draws the projection plane more explicitly, but its box is offset so the pinhole lies on an edge/corner of the rear face rather than centered, making the optical axis and focal-length segment hit an edge of the projection plane rather than the central camera geometry required by the brief (L00010). Both figures are weakened because the labeled Z/optical axis points away from the drawn projection plane rather than forward from the pinhole toward the front face, so Figure 1 wins only by being less geometrically misleading overall (L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it preserves the intended pinhole-camera geometry and recognizable 3D textbook composition: the camera body, projection plane, pinhole, focal-length arrow, and axes are more correctly aligned and visually faithful than in Figure 2. Figure 2 has clearer labels and much better requested interactivity, but its pinhole/optical-axis geometry is substantially more misleading, with the camera box shifted so the pinhole lies near an edge or corner and the principal axis misses the projection-plane center.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the epipolar geometry: its camera centers, image planes, projections, epipoles, epipolar lines, projection rays, baseline segment, and epipolar plane are all tied together by consistent camera-local projection geometry. Figure 2 includes more 3D embellishments such as frustums and thick cylinders, but its dashed baseline is a long fixed world line rather than the actual O1–O2 segment, its epipoles are often far outside the finite image planes due to the chosen plane scale/yaw, and the perspective viewpoint/proportions make it less like a clean textbook construction.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 is better because its advertised interactions directly drive the live epipolar model: dragging P updates p1, p2, the epipolar plane, projection rays, epipoles, and epipolar lines, and the baseline/Camera 2 rotation sliders recompute the geometry consistently. Figure 2's sliders do update much of the scene, but it does not provide true 3D dragging of P, only a one-dimensional Point P X slider, and its baseline line is a static long line rather than a recomputed O1-O2 segment, so the visual baseline interaction is less correct; its step buttons work but also animate the sliders rather than adding a more faithful manipulation.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is recognizable as the epipolar-geometry diagram, with two camera/image planes, a yellow epipolar plane, red projection/epipolar lines, labeled points P, p1/p2, e1/e2, O1/O2, and a dashed baseline, whereas Figure 2 does not render the figure at all and only shows a load failure message.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 at least renders the main labels such as P, epipolar plane, epipolar line, Camera 1/2, O1/O2, p1/p2, and e labels, though several are too small, cluttered, or misplaced compared with the reference. Figure 2 fails to load entirely, so it has no usable labels or annotations.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more faithfully represents the core epipolar geometry: P projects to p1 and p2, O1-P-O2 defines the epipolar plane, the epipoles are computed as projections/intersections of the opposite camera center with each image plane, and the epipolar lines are drawn through the epipoles and image projections as required (L00007, L00012-L00015, L00018). Figure 2 gets most of the same geometry right, but its baseline-control tooltip asserts that changing only the camera distance shifts the epipoles; for a fixed baseline direction and yaw-only setup, the epipole as an image point is determined by the direction of the other camera center, not the baseline length, so that statement can teach a wrong limiting behavior relative to the epipole definition (L00007, L00018).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner: it renders a recognizable epipolar-geometry construction with labeled cameras, image planes, projections, epipoles, epipolar lines, baseline, and epipolar plane, while Figure 2 reportedly fails to render in the screenshot-based evaluations and therefore lacks usable labels or visual faithfulness. Even from the source-code evaluations, Figure 1 has more consistent camera-local projection geometry and interactions that update P, projections, epipoles, rays, and planes coherently, whereas Figure 2 has a static/incorrect baseline representation, less faithful point manipulation, and a misleading baseline-length claim about epipole behavior.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the original decoder diagram’s row-wise structure: all seven token rows pass through embeddings, masked-attention transformer internals, residual addition nodes, feed-forward blocks, linear/softmax, and probability vectors with arrowheads. Figure 2 captures the broad left-to-right pipeline but collapses much of the transformer into a single central path, omits per-row residual/addition topology through the transformer, uses fewer embedding cells, and represents repeated layers mainly as background stacking/text rather than maintaining the full repeated node-and-edge structure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the requested controls much more correctly: its K slider updates the displayed value and redraws the architecture with the selected number of transformer blocks, its block overlays support hover tooltips and click popups for embeddings, transformer, residual additions, linear/softmax, and probability outputs, and its trace animation follows the final input row through attention, residuals, linear/softmax, and the “yourself” output. Figure 2 has several interaction faults: the K slider redraws only background stack hints and leaves the numeric output stale, the advertised click-on-block interaction is mostly missing because there are no click handlers and the transformer tooltip is attached to an empty group, probability and residual blocks are not individually interactive, and the “yourself” trace is more of a temporary highlight than a proper path animation.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the full left-to-right composition of the original, including the word embedding grids, masked attention block, repeated decoder structure, linear/softmax outputs, and probability-token bars with a similar color scheme. Figure 2 has the same general layout but is more stripped down: the word embeddings are largely missing or reduced to an empty dashed column, the probability distribution bars are mostly absent, and there is an extraneous small element near the upper left, making it less immediately recognizable as the textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 preserves more of the original labeling scheme, including the input tokens, section titles, output token names, and bottom vocabulary annotations, with placements that generally correspond to the reference. Figure 2 has noticeably poorer label fidelity: the word-embedding area is partially broken with a stray unlabeled embedding row, several labels are smaller and harder to read, and some required annotations are missing or displaced compared with the original.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the decoder-only transformer: it shows every token position carrying its own representation through masked attention, residual/addition nodes, repeated decoder processing, Linear + softmax, and shifted targets from <start>→It through let→yourself, matching the parallel next-token prediction and causal masking described in the brief (L00007). Figure 2 gets the lower-triangular causal mask largely right, but its main transformer-to-linear flow is drawn as a single central pathway that fans out to all output rows, which can falsely suggest one representation produces all positions rather than each processed token representation feeding its own classifier (L00007); its “yourself” animation also highlights a probability cell aligned with the displayed vocabulary label “zeta,” creating a misleading assertion about the target token’s vocabulary probability (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear winner because it preserves the decoder diagram’s row-wise token flow through embeddings, masked attention, residual/addition nodes, feed-forward/repeated blocks, linear-softmax, and per-token probability outputs, while Figure 2 collapses much of this into a simplified central pathway that weakens both the geometry and the conceptual message. Figure 1 also implements the intended interactions more fully, including a functioning K slider, tooltips/click popups, and a trace animation, whereas Figure 2 has stale slider output, mostly missing click behavior, and a less accurate highlight. Visually and textually, Figure 1 better matches the reference labels, tokens, output annotations, and probability bars, while Figure 2 omits or displaces several of these elements and includes stray or misleading details.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the likely textbook structure: it keeps a static pinhole-camera scene with two free-space sample points shown by dense radial incoming rays and two inside-camera sample points reached by single sparse rays that pass through the pinhole. Figure 2 preserves the general idea but alters the layout more substantially, lowers and reshapes the camera, uses two aperture-edge rays per inside point rather than a single sparse ray through the pinhole, and adds dynamic relocation behavior that changes the intended fixed structural arrangement.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the requested interaction much more correctly: clicking or dragging moves a sampling point and recomputes/redraws its dense or sparse angular ray distribution based on whether it is inside the camera, and its direct controls move all points between free-space and camera states. Figure 1’s controls mostly only fade predrawn ray groups or step through narration; its sampling points cannot be moved by clicking anywhere, and clicking a dot only opens explanatory text rather than updating the plenoptic distribution, so it misses the main advertised interaction.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable as the original because it preserves the key composition of a pinhole camera on the left, two red sample points with radiating rays in the middle, and a tree on the right, with visible connecting rays from the scene toward the camera. Figure 2 has the same basic elements, but its ray structure is more simplified and clustered, with fewer long directional rays, making it read less like the original plenoptic ray diagram and more like isolated sunburst markers beside a tree.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the required 'Pinhole camera' label in a clearer, larger, more readable placement above the box, closer to the reference. Figure 1 also includes the label, but it is smaller and bolder at inline size, and its side panel adds more prominent invented instructional labels such as a title, step indicator, and view mode that are not in the original, creating more label clutter than Figure 2.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately preserves the required conceptual setup of exactly four sampled spatial locations with two in free space and two inside a pinhole camera (L00017, L00022-L00028), and it shows the camera samples as sparse with a single specific ray direction through the pinhole, matching the idea that most directions are zero inside the camera (L00024-L00025, L00028). Figure 2 also conveys dense free-space directions and sparse camera directions, but its controls and demo states move all four samples into free space or all into the camera, which contradicts the stated two-and-two sampling arrangement, and its finite-aperture two-edge rays are less faithful to a pinhole camera’s specific-direction behavior than Figure 1’s single-ray depiction.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 better preserves the core textbook diagram: a static pinhole-camera setup with two free-space samples shown by dense incoming rays and two camera-interior samples shown by sparse single rays through the pinhole, making it both conceptually and geometrically closer to the intended figure. Figure 2 has stronger interactive behavior and a clearer camera label, but relative to Figure 1 it simplifies and clusters the ray structure, changes the camera/sample arrangement, and its all-free-space/all-camera control states and two-edge aperture rays undermine the intended two-and-two pinhole sampling concept.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better preserves the likely original static structure of the sigmoid textbook plot: the boxed axes, -5/0/5 and 0/1 labels, the orange sigmoid curve, the dashed guide lines to (0, 0.5), and the fraction annotation appear without extra default marks. Figure 1 has accurate axis ranges and a good curve, but it introduces an always-visible blue threshold L-line, a large highlighted point, and a coordinate readout that add non-original structure and make the reconstruction less faithful despite its more accurate inward tick styling.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the intended point interaction more correctly: the user can actually click and drag within the plot to move the point along the sigmoid, with the coordinate readout recomputed from the current z value. Figure 1 only provides a z slider rather than a draggable point, so it reaches a similar state but does not match the advertised interaction as directly. For the threshold control, both recompute the inverse sigmoid correctly over the slider range, but Figure 2 additionally marks and labels the z intercept, whereas Figure 1 only draws a dashed drop-line without an explicit intercept marker or z readout.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it preserves the original’s clean sigmoid plot with light gray dotted guide lines, similar formula annotation, axes, and overall composition. Figure 1 has the same basic sigmoid shape, but the bright blue dashed guides, added point marker, and coordinate label introduce prominent elements not present in the textbook figure, making it look less like the original at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 better matches the original labeling because it includes the key formula and axis labels without adding the extra coordinate annotation that Figure 1 places on the curve. Figure 1's required labels are readable, but the invented “(0.00, 0.50)” label and additional control text make it less faithful and more cluttered; Figure 2 is closer overall despite its tick labels being somewhat tight against the plot edges.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 is slightly more conceptually accurate because it correctly plots the logistic sigmoid over z∈[−5,5], states the open (0,1) squashing behavior, and explicitly describes the steepest region at z=0 with sig[z]=0.5, matching the main mathematical ideas in the brief (L00007). Figure 1 also uses the correct sigmoid formula and curve, but its always-visible threshold/drop-line overlay at 0.5 makes the reference structure more confusing; both figures are inaccurate relative to the requested gray dashed horizontal asymptote at sig[z]=1.0 because they instead draw a dashed horizontal guide at sig[z]=0.5, but Figure 2’s other annotations are less likely to reinforce that wrong asymptote cue (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the clear overall winner because it more faithfully preserves the clean textbook sigmoid plot, including the boxed axes, orange curve, formula annotation, and light guide lines, while Figure 1 adds prominent non-original elements such as a blue threshold line, large point marker, and coordinate readout. It also better matches the intended interaction by allowing the point to be dragged along the curve, whereas Figure 1 substitutes a slider for that interaction. Although both have some conceptual issues around the dashed guide/asymptote cue, Figure 2’s annotations and structure are less cluttered and less misleading relative to Figure 1.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the likely textbook geometry because it preserves a continuous square image plane subdivided into regular 4×4, 2×2, and 1×1 window partitions with internal token gridlines and consistent proportions. Figure 2 instead reduces the image to an 8×8 set of thick extruded cubes, explodes windows apart with artificial gaps, and its “4×4 windows” correspond to only 2×2-token groups, so the element counts and spatial relationships are less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2's slider, offset checkbox, and click interaction all update the live token layout consistently, preserve/recompute the selected token's attention window when the partition changes, and behave sensibly at the 1×1 degenerate case. Figure 1's main controls mostly work visually, but every rebuild registers new clickable tile meshes without unregistering the old removed ones, so after changing window size or offset the raycaster can hit stale invisible tiles and draw/highlight an outdated window; it also clears the selected attention demonstration on every partition change rather than showing how the same locality changes under offset.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more visually faithful because it preserves the key idea of the reference: a graffiti-wall image with a cartoon figure, red writing, and visible window/grid partitioning in perspective. Figure 2 only shows abstract colored tile groups for 4×4 windows and loses the photographic/graffiti content and overall composition, making it far less recognizable as the same textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has a clear, readable label '4×4 windows' placed under the rendered window grid, matching one of the original captions, whereas Figure 1 lacks the original-style caption under the artwork and instead relies on small UI/demo text that is not part of the textbook figure. Both figures omit most required labels such as panel letters and the other window captions, but Figure 1 adds more irrelevant interface annotations and its label text is less directly aligned with the original.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more conceptually accurate because it represents the image as a continuous photograph texture cut into separated window tiles for 4×4, shifted 4×4, 2×2, shifted 2×2, and 1×1 cases, and its narration explicitly states that shifted windows allow tokens formerly separated by boundaries to communicate while retaining local attention efficiency, matching the Swin shifted-window strategy (L00007). Figure 2 correctly conveys local attention within windows and supports regular/offset and 1×1/2×2/4×4 states, but it reduces the photograph to independent token blocks and does not clearly teach the alternating-layer boundary-crossing strategy; its “Partition Size” wording is also less precise because the brief’s captions describe the number of windows across the image, not a generic partition size (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it preserves the recognizable graffiti/image-plane composition and the correct continuous grid/window geometry, while Figure 2 abstracts the scene into separated colored blocks with less faithful element counts and spatial relationships. Figure 1 also better conveys the shifted-window concept and boundary-crossing idea, whereas Figure 2 is comparatively weaker conceptually despite having cleaner labels and more robust interactive behavior. geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the structural layout of a pinhole-projection diagram: it uses thin pixel-strip rows, a fuller fan of blocked red rays plus the transmitted ray, correctly reversed sensor indexing, and arrowhead markers oriented along diagonal rays. geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the full 3D BRDF geometry: it has the large surface plane, origin marker, correctly scaled n/p/q basis arrows, incoming ray with its tip at the surface, and a dense hemispherical set of outgoing rays that forms a plausible scattering lobe. Figure 2 captures the same basic components but its outgoing distribution is much sparser and more schematic, the p/q tangent axes appear swapped relative to Figure 1’s more coherent basis layout, and the initial orthographic setup is less reliably framed because the camera view is set before the full scene is constructed.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the requested incoming-ray drag and recomputes the outgoing BRDF lobe and labels continuously from the dragged direction and material sliders, including handling near-horizon directions with a clamp. Figure 1’s sliders and material buttons do recompute the lobe correctly for many states, but it lacks the direct ray-drag interaction and its direction control is more limited/mislabeled as elevation while actually behaving like polar angle from the normal; it also has a weaker material model with diffuse largely unaffected by incoming direction.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is much more recognizable as the reference: it includes the green surface, diagonal incoming yellow/orange light ray, outgoing green direction with the formula label, normal, p/q directions, and several diffuse green rays around the contact point. Figure 1 has the green plane and a normal/p/q setup, but the incoming light is nearly vertical rather than diagonal, the outgoing/diffuse structure is largely absent, and the overall composition reads more like a simplified lighting demo than the original diagram.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has substantially more readable and complete annotations: l_in(λ), l_out=F(l_in, n, λ, p, q), and p/n/q are visible and placed near the corresponding vectors. Figure 1 includes similar labels, but they are extremely small and mostly illegible at the rendered size, with the main formula compressed into tiny text near the center, making it much poorer for label quality.

concept.rationale: Both figures incorrectly label p and q as tangent coordinate axes rather than the incident and outgoing ray directions used by the BRDF equation, so both risk teaching a false relationship among n, p, and q (L00009-L00017). Figure 2 is still more conceptually accurate because its outgoing distribution implements a diffuse term that is independent of viewing direction aside from the incident cosine factor and a specular term controlled by material parameters, matching the general diffuse/specular BRDF idea better (L00020-L00030). Figure 1 does show a hemisphere of scattered outgoing rays, but its 'Diffuse' mode makes diffuse outgoing intensity vary with the outgoing direction n·q, contradicting the Lambertian formula where q does not appear, and its glossy lobe omits the incident-angle cosine dependence emphasized for diffuse reflection (L00024-L00030).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the clearer overall match: compared with Figure 1, it more faithfully resembles the rendered reference, has readable labels for the incoming ray, outgoing BRDF expression, and p/n/q directions, and implements the key interaction of dragging the incoming ray with continuous lobe updates. Figure 1 has stronger source-level 3D geometry with a denser hemisphere and more coherent basis layout, but relative to Figure 2 it is visually less faithful, its labels are mostly illegible, it lacks direct ray dragging, and its diffuse behavior is less conceptually accurate.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the geometric structure of the translation diagram: it keeps a uniform x/y scale so the squares remain square and the vector directions/proportions are accurate, and it shows the full topology of original square, translated square(s), red directed vectors t, s, and t+s with the homogeneous matrix relation in the figure area. Figure 2 has the same basic node/vector count, but its plot-frame scaling can distort world units differently in x and y, making squares into rectangles and altering vector angles; it also moves the matrices into the UI and omits the matrix relation from the main drawing, making the reconstructed 2D textbook structure less faithful.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 has more fully working controls: dragging and sliders both recompute the square positions, vectors, displayed coordinate values, and homogeneous/composed matrices, and its redraw clears labels so degenerate zero-length vectors do not leave stale annotations. Figure 1’s drag and mode controls mostly work and its matrix updates, but exact zero translations can leave the previous vector label stranded because positionLabel returns without clearing or hiding it, and dragging t in chained mode can push the composed final square off the visible frame; it also offers less direct control coverage than Figure 2.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because its main drawing uses the same clean black axes, large orange squares with black outlines, red translation arrow, and italic x/y/t labeling style seen in the textbook figure. Figure 1 has the same basic elements, but the added grid, much smaller scale, gray axes, and floating matrix box make it look more like a plotted interactive diagram than the original textbook illustration.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the required diagram labels x, y, and t in larger, clearer, better-placed italic text that more closely matches the reference, while Figure 1 includes the same labels but they are noticeably smaller and less readable at inline size. Figure 2 does introduce more extra interface text in the side panel, but the actual figure annotations are superior; Figure 1 also has invented UI/matrix text and does not compensate with equally readable diagram labels.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly show a square translated by vector t and, when chained, a second translation s with a direct t+s arrow, matching the additive rule for translations (L00007-L00023, L00026, L00053-L00054). Figure 2 is slightly better conceptually because it explicitly labels the component values t_x, t_y, s_x, s_y and shows the homogeneous matrices with the composed S·T translation entries equal to the coordinate sums, directly supporting the homogeneous-coordinate composition point (L00028-L00030, L00041-L00048). Figure 1 is also essentially correct, but its component relationship is less explicit in the main graphic and its intended left/right comparison is replaced by a stepped overlay, making the same concepts somewhat less directly established.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall: compared with Figure 1 it more closely matches the textbook rendering with clean axes, large orange outlined squares, readable italic x/y/t labels, and more complete working controls that update coordinates, vectors, and homogeneous/composed matrices. Figure 1 has the notable geometric advantage of preserving uniform scale and embedding the matrix relation in the drawing, while Figure 2 may distort square proportions through plot-frame scaling; however, Figure 1 is visually less faithful, has smaller labels, less direct control coverage, and some interaction edge cases such as stale labels or objects moving off-frame.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better matches the projective-geometry construction: it shows four rays emanating from O as rays rather than full infinite lines, places P and Q point sets cleanly on their transversals, and represents R1 at infinity by putting the R1 → ∞ label on/near the R transversal that is parallel to the first ray. Figure 1 has the same basic topology, but its black rays are drawn as full lines through O, its P points are comparatively compressed, and most importantly its R1 → ∞ label is placed along the first ray far from the R line, which makes the infinity construction structurally misleading.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the core requested interactions: O and the P/Q/R point handles recompute the projected rays and intersections, and the displayed cross-ratio values update in real time; Figure 2 only lets O, P points, and transversals move, with no cross-ratio display at all and no draggable Q or R points despite the brief. Figure 2's O movement is also artificially clamped, while Figure 1 allows arbitrary center dragging, though Figure 1 is not perfect because R points at infinity become hidden and cannot themselves be dragged directly.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it preserves the original composition at a glance: O on the left, four rays fanning right, two magenta transversals for P and Q, and the magenta R line with R1 toward infinity on the right. Figure 1 has the same conceptual elements but is much more compressed, uses thinner/smaller marks and labels, and its displayed configuration makes R1 appear as a separate infinity state rather than matching the original layout as closely.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has the required diagram labels O, P1–P4, Q1–Q4, R1→∞, and R2–R4 with mostly correct text and relatively clear placement, whereas Figure 2 omits the infinity on R1 and has more crowding/overlap in the central cluster, especially around P4/Q4 and R4. Figure 1’s labels are somewhat small, but Figure 2’s label placement is less faithful and more cluttered.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more directly and correctly represents the projective-invariance claim by showing four rays from O intersecting three collinear point sets P, Q, and R and by displaying the same cross-ratio value for the projected sets, matching the brief’s statement that collinear sets related by projection preserve cross-ratio when ordered consistently (L00010). It also explicitly handles R1 as a point at infinity when the R line is parallel to the ray through O, P1, and Q1 (L00007, L00010). Figure 2’s geometry is mostly correct for the projection and R1-at-infinity condition, but it teaches the cross-ratio less concretely because it asserts preservation without showing or calculating the cross-ratio relationship, so a student gets less direct confirmation of the invariant described in the brief (L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it implements the key interactive behavior and conceptual teaching goal that Figure 2 lacks: draggable projected points with recomputed intersections and live cross-ratio values, making the projective-invariance claim explicit rather than merely implied. It also labels the required P, Q, and R points, including R1→∞, more completely, whereas Figure 2 omits or crowds important labels and has no cross-ratio display or draggable Q/R points. Figure 2 has a cleaner rendered construction and more faithful ray geometry, but those advantages do not outweigh Figure 1’s superior coverage of the intended interaction and mathematical message.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the full 3D projection setup: it models the L-shaped block as a true extruded stair-step solid, places it at a controlled distance from a projection plane, computes the flattened projection onto that plane, and draws projection rays from the object to the plane. Figure 2 has the same basic elements but is more schematic: the projected shape is hard-coded as two colored rectangles rather than a true computed projection of the solid, it shows fewer projection rays, and its face/projection coloring and spatial mapping are less faithful to the likely textbook geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements and wires up substantially more of the requested interactions: the distance slider moves the object and recomputes rays/projection, the projection-type control switches to a foreshortened perspective-style projection, and the depth-guide toggle at least updates visible guide geometry. Figure 2’s single distance slider mostly works for the orthographic case, but it does not provide any orthographic-to-perspective comparison or depth-guide toggle, and its projected shape remains static because it only demonstrates the orthographic case. Figure 1 is not perfect—the perspective projection formula has a ternary/precedence bug that can collapse some projected coordinates at certain slider values, and its depth guides are incomplete—but it still offers more working intended interaction than Figure 2.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it clearly preserves the two separated red rectangular blocks, green top faces, cyan side face, dashed projection guides, labeled axes, and projection plane arrangement seen in the reference. Figure 1 has the same general idea but the object is much less recognizable: the colored block structure is compressed/simplified, the green top surfaces are mostly absent, and the projected/guide geometry reads less like the original composition.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has clearer, larger, and better placed diagram labels: X, Y, Z and “Projection plane” are readable and mostly separated from the artwork. Figure 1’s labels are much smaller, the “Projection plane” text is crowded into the plane/axis area, and the screenshot contains many extra UI annotation labels on the right that are not part of the original figure and add clutter.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more accurately teaches the core orthographic relationship: the object moves along the displayed Z/projection direction, the dashed rays remain parallel and perpendicular to the projection plane, and the projected L-shape stays fixed in lateral size as distance changes, matching x=X, y=Y and distance-independent orthographic projection (L00007, L00010). Figure 1 also has parallel orthographic rays and constant-size projection, but it renders the projected object essentially all red rather than preserving the color-face layout of the red/green/cyan staircase on the plane, so it is less faithful to the stated projected-shape claim (L00010). Figure 2 is not perfect because its projected colors are still simplified, but it is conceptually closer than Figure 1.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the stronger overall match because it more clearly preserves the intended orthographic teaching: readable axes and projection-plane labels, separated colored block faces, dashed parallel projection guides, and a distance-independent projected shape. Figure 1 has a more robust computed 3D setup and more implemented controls, but relative to Figure 2 it is visually less faithful, more cluttered, less readable, and its projected/color-face representation is less aligned with the stated concept.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the likely textbook geometry by using an oblique/front-on projection with mapped axes so Y is vertical, Z is horizontal, and X recedes diagonally, and it keeps the camera frame, image plane, local axes, rotation arrows, projection point, and drop line spatially coherent under Euler rotations. Figure 2 uses a perspective camera with a different viewpoint and proportions, much larger axes/plane, and largely static rotation arrows, so the printed diagram’s oblique layout and rotating-frame relationships are less accurately reconstructed.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1’s sliders, rotation-order toggle, and sequence animation more cleanly recompute the camera frame, projected point, labels, and active-axis highlighting, and it supports a wider roll range without the animation lingering in a no-highlight state. Figure 2’s core sliders and order toggle also work, but its roll control is unnecessarily narrowed to ±90°, its stop/animation behavior can jump back to the full target orientation rather than preserving the current animated state, and its projected-point hiding/label handling is less robust than Figure 1’s offscreen-position approach.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is much more recognizable as the reference: it includes the central translucent plane, black coordinate axes, red yaw/pitch/roll rotation arcs, green local x/y vectors, labeled points p and P, and dashed/projection geometry in roughly the same conceptual arrangement. Figure 1 shows only a very sparse pale 3D skeleton with a point and dashed lines, with most of the defining visual elements from the original missing or too faint to read, so it does not resemble the textbook figure nearly as well.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has substantially better label coverage: it includes visible axis labels, point labels, and yaw/pitch/roll annotations in approximately relevant locations, whereas Figure 1’s diagram labels are largely missing, extremely tiny, or collapsed/clipped in the bottom-left corner and do not annotate the main artwork. Figure 2’s labels are still smaller than the reference and not all textbook labels such as θX/θY/θZ and coordinate labels are clearly reproduced, but it is far more readable and complete than Figure 1.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more truthfully represents the Euler-angle camera-rotation setup: its labeled camera axes, image plane, local image axes, and p projection rotate together, so yaw is about Y, pitch about X, and roll about Z within the camera-frame decomposition, while still showing P and the projection ray geometry (L00007-L00011, L00014). Figure 2 correctly labels the three nominal rotation types and projection elements, but its main X/Y/Z axes and red rotation arrows remain essentially static while the image plane rotates, which can teach that the Euler sequence is about fixed displayed axes rather than the camera frame being related to the world frame; it therefore represents the relationship among axes, frame rotation, and projection less accurately (L00014).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because its source-level geometry and behavior more accurately maintain the camera frame, image plane, projected point, local axes, and Euler rotation relationships, whereas Figure 2 presents more static axes/arrows and can imply rotations about fixed displayed axes rather than the rotating camera frame. Figure 2 is clearly better as a rendered reproduction, with more recognizable visual elements and readable labels, while Figure 1 is visually sparse and poorly labeled; however, the higher number of geometry/interactivity/concept advantages gives Figure 1 the slight overall edge.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 reconstructs the pinhole-camera geometry more accurately: it places the camera center at the origin, uses a coherent optical axis with virtual and sensor planes at +f and -f, includes a full 3D house volume with roof, ray, intersections, rectangular sensor grid, pixel highlight, and dimension brackets. Figure 2 has a more schematic and partially flattened house made mostly from planes, uses a square N×N sensor despite labeling M pixels, snaps pixels by rounding rather than true binning, and remaps the camera axes/optical direction in a way that is less faithful to the typical source geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 has more consistently correct handlers: dragging P recomputes the ray, virtual projection, sensor projection, snapped pixel highlight, grid, and readout together, and its slider extremes are bounded and out-of-bounds projections are explicitly handled. Figure 2 does update its sliders, readout, and intrinsic matrix, but at extreme focal length/sensor-width/drag positions it can place the snapped pixel and report pixel indices outside the sensor without warning, so its advertised discretization interaction breaks down more readily; it also relies on a more restricted drag plane and has less robust boundary behavior than Figure 1.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is much more visually faithful because it preserves the reference’s left-to-right layout of sensor/image plane, camera center/virtual image plane, optical axis, and colored 3D object, with similar labels and coordinate arrows. Figure 1 includes some of the same ingredients, but its composition is reversed and compressed, the UI dominates the screenshot, and the diagram lacks the clear optical-axis/plane/object arrangement that makes the original recognizable at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 includes many of the textbook labels directly on the diagram, such as Image plane / sensor, N pixels, M pixels, Camera center, Virtual image plane, optical/principal axis, Xc/Yc/Zc, P, w, and f, with generally readable placement. Figure 1 has very few usable diagram labels at inline size and instead includes many unrelated UI/control labels and explanatory text that are not part of the original figure, while the actual annotations in the 3D view are tiny and hard to read.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more concept-accurate because it represents the optical axis as Zc from the pinhole, puts the virtual image plane at +f and the physical sensor at -f, and computes the virtual and sensor intersections with the expected perspective scaling, while Figure 2 uses a less direct coordinate remapping that is mostly workable but easier to misread (L00015). More importantly, Figure 1 renders an N-by-M sensor grid by deriving M separately from N, whereas Figure 2 explicitly labels the resolution as N×N and uses a square grid even though the context and brief specify an N×M / M-by-N sensor (L00012, L00015). Figure 2 does better at showing a numeric intrinsic matrix, but its square-sensor assertion is a direct conceptual mismatch, while Figure 1’s main weakness is less explicit labeling of pixel size and principal point offset rather than a false relationship (L00015).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because its source-level construction more accurately implements the pinhole-camera geometry, N-by-M sensor grid, perspective intersections, and interactive updates, while Figure 2 has a square-grid/resolution mismatch and less robust boundary behavior for snapped pixel indices. Figure 2 is clearly better as a rendered textbook-style diagram, with more recognizable layout and readable labels, but those visual advantages do not outweigh Figure 1’s more correct geometry, concept, and interaction behavior.
